opus-5.5.text:
Well, the way I like to think about it is that it's actually a very old idea wearing new clothes. If you look at the planning and search literature, there's this classic "generate and test" paradigm: you have a generator that proposes candidates, and a tester that checks them. The LLM, in my view, is a wonderful generator. It's an approximate retrieval engine that can throw out plausible-looking candidates at a remarkable rate. But plausible is not the same as correct.

So when people say "inference-time scaling," and they mean "let's sample the LLM many times and pick the best," the first question I always ask is: *who is doing the picking?* That's where all the action is. If you have a sound external verifier, say a plan validator, a compiler, a unit test suite, a theorem checker, then generating many candidates and filtering them is a perfectly principled thing to do. That's essentially what we argued for in the LLM-Modulo framework: let the LLM guess, and let verifiers with actual guarantees do the checking, with critiques fed back to the generator. In that setting, more samples genuinely buy you more accuracy, because you're increasing the chance that some candidate lands in the correct region, and the verifier will recognize it when it does.

The trouble comes when the verifier is itself the LLM, or a learned reward model, or just majority voting. Self-consistency and majority voting assume that the correct answer is the mode of the distribution. That holds for some kinds of problems, but there's no general reason to believe it. And having the LLM critique its own answers, as we showed in some of our work on self-verification for planning and graph coloring, often doesn't help and can even hurt. The model is as likely to reject a correct answer as to accept a wrong one. So you can scale compute all you want, but if your selection mechanism is unsound, you're mostly paying for more expensive guessing.

Here's the other point I'd stress. There's a tendency to anthropomorphize this, to say the model is "thinking longer" and therefore "reasoning more." I'd be careful there. Drawing more samples or producing longer intermediate token sequences doesn't by itself mean there's reasoning going on in the sense we use in AI, with guarantees about correctness. It's compute being spent on search, and search is great! I'm a planning person, I love search. But let's call it what it is and ask where the soundness comes from.

There's also a cost-benefit question people tend to skip. If you need, say, a hundred samples plus a verifier to solve a problem that a classical solver handles in milliseconds with guarantees, then the more interesting question is when the LLM's generality is worth that overhead. Sometimes it is, especially when the domain doesn't have a formal model and the LLM's broad knowledge helps you get candidates at all. But it isn't a free lunch.

So in short: I see multiple-candidate inference-time scaling as a generate-and-test loop. Its value is bounded by the quality of the tester. With a good verifier it's powerful and principled. Without one, it's mostly hope, at scale.

r001.rationale: The response says the LLM proposes plausible candidates that may be incorrect and distinguishes that from sound verification with correctness guarantees.

r002.rationale: It describes sampling the LLM many times and selecting among candidates, including self-consistency and majority voting, as inference-time scaling.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the way I think about it is actually quite simple, and I think it demystifies a lot of what's being sold as "reasoning." If you take an LLM and sample from it many times, you're essentially using it as a generator. It's a very good generator, a very good idea generator, because it has this enormous prior over what plausible-looking answers for a given prompt tend to be. But generation is only half of the problem. The other half is verification. Somebody has to tell you which of those candidates is actually correct.

So when people say inference-time scaling, what they're really doing, in the cleanest case, is what we called LLM-Modulo back in our work. You have the LLM throwing out candidates, and then you have something external, a verifier, that checks them. In a planning problem, that verifier might be a model-based plan validator like VAL. In math, it might be a symbolic checker or a unit test. If the verifier is sound, then generating more candidates strictly increases your chance that one of them passes, and the whole thing is correct by construction, because the correctness is coming from the verifier, not from the LLM.

The confusion starts when the verifier is also an LLM, or when there's no real verifier at all and you're just doing majority voting over the samples. Majority voting only works if the model's errors are somehow uncorrelated and the right answer is the mode, and there's no principled reason to believe that in general. We've seen cases where the LLM confidently converges on the same wrong answer ten times out of ten. More samples just give you a more confident wrong answer.

And this is why I keep harping on the distinction between the language model being an approximate retriever versus a reasoner. The sampling gives you candidates that look like solutions. Whether they are solutions depends entirely on who's doing the checking. The so-called reasoning models, the ones trained with RL on verifiable outcomes, are in some sense internalizing a part of this loop during training, so the generator gets better at producing candidates that tend to pass the verifier. That's fine, that's useful. But it doesn't change the epistemology. You still want to know, at the end, whether the thing was checked by something that actually knows the answer, or whether you just took the LLM's word for it enough times that it started to sound convincing.

r001.rationale: The response says sampled outputs are candidates that only look like solutions and that correctness depends on verification, so generation alone provides no correctness guarantee.

r002.rationale: It connects inference-time scaling with sampling multiple candidates and explicitly discusses majority voting over those samples as an approach.

astra-6.text:
I think the useful way to understand it is as a generate-and-test process. Instead of asking the language model for one answer, you give it more computation to produce multiple candidates. But then the crucial question is: how do you decide which candidate to accept?

Generating a correct answer somewhere among a hundred candidates is different from knowing which one is correct. If you have a reliable verifier—say, you can execute a proposed solution and check whether it satisfies the requirements—then additional sampling can be very useful. The language model supplies proposals, and the verifier supplies the grounds for accepting them.

If you ask the same model to choose its best answer, you have to establish that its ability to recognize correctness is actually better than its ability to generate a correct answer. You cannot simply assume that. And majority voting establishes agreement among samples; it doesn't establish truth. The samples can share the same mistake.

So inference-time scaling can buy you more opportunities to find a solution. Whether those opportunities translate into reliable performance depends on the selection mechanism, the diversity of the candidates, and the feedback available. That's where I would put the emphasis: what is doing the checking?

r001.rationale: The response says that generating a correct answer among many candidates does not establish which one is correct, and that majority agreement does not establish truth.

r002.rationale: The response describes producing multiple candidates as inference-time scaling, but does not identify aggregating those candidates as a form of scaling; majority voting is mentioned only as an unreliable way to judge them.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that you’re moving from generating an answer to searching over possible answers. Instead of asking the model once, you let it produce multiple candidates, perhaps with different intermediate steps, and then you need some way of deciding which candidate to accept.

And that second part is crucial. Generating more candidates is useful if you have a reliable way to recognize a good one. If you’re writing code and you have meaningful tests, or solving a problem where you can check the constraints, then additional inference compute can improve your chances of finding a valid solution. The language model is providing proposals; the checker is providing the grounds for accepting them.

But if you ask the same model to generate ten answers and then judge which one is correct, you haven’t automatically acquired a reliable verifier. The answers can share the same mistake, and the model can prefer a persuasive explanation over a correct one. Majority voting can help in some settings, but agreement is not a certificate of correctness.

So I would ask: What is the search space, how diverse are the candidates, and where does the verification come from? Inference-time scaling gives you more opportunities to find a good answer. Whether those opportunities translate into dependable reasoning depends very much on how you evaluate and select the answers.

r001.rationale: It says candidates can share the same mistake and that model agreement is not a certificate of correctness, so they carry no correctness guarantee.

r002.rationale: It describes generating multiple candidates and selecting among them, explicitly mentioning majority voting as a way to aggregate them within inference-time scaling.
